Chapter 2: Holding On and Letting Go—Family Bonds in Changing Times.
Every family has its own rhythm, doesn’t it? There are those daily routines, the inside jokes you whisper across the table, and all those little unspoken rules that just seem to fall into place.
But what happens when life changes? When kids grow up, or the world just...shifts? The father’s letters to Su Yen are like gentle reminders, filled with thoughts on how to keep those family ties strong, even as everyone’s lives start moving in different directions.
He looks back on the early days—those big, noisy family gatherings, where laughter echoed through the house, plates piled high with food, and yes, the occasional disagreement. There was a comfort in knowing exactly what to expect. No matter what chaos waited outside, home always felt like a place to belong.
But as time passed, things changed. Work, school, and new adventures called everyone away. The dinner table, once crowded and lively, grew quieter. Traditions that used to feel unbreakable started to slip away, almost without anyone noticing.
And here’s where the father gets real. It’s so easy to let a little distance become a big excuse for drifting apart. You miss a call, you forget a birthday...and suddenly, the distance feels huge. He tells Su Yen about a cousin who moved overseas, promising to stay in touch, but slowly faded from the family’s everyday life. When they finally reconnected years later, both felt the ache of time lost—a powerful reminder that relationships need care, even when life gets hectic.
He also talks about the challenge of holding onto tradition when everything around you is changing so fast. He remembers his own parents, who insisted on celebrating certain festivals, honoring elders, and speaking their native language at home. Back then, those rules seemed strict—maybe even outdated. But now, he sees how those traditions gave him a sense of identity and a place to stand when things felt uncertain.
Now, as Su Yen grows up in a multicultural world, the big question is: How do you balance honoring where you come from, with the freedom to find your own way? The father encourages her to see family customs not as heavy burdens, but as gifts—guides to help her understand both her roots and her future. Still, he’s honest: some traditions might need to change, and it’s okay to let go of what no longer fits.
He shares a memory of a family disagreement over whether to keep an old holiday ritual. Some wanted to stick with what they knew; others wanted something new. In the end, they found a way to blend both—honoring their past while opening the door to new traditions. And in that moment, it became clear: what really makes a family strong isn’t rigidly sticking to the old ways, but being willing to adapt together.
Through all these stories, the father’s message is gentle but clear. Family bonds aren’t automatic—they take effort, patience, and a lot of forgiveness. There will be misunderstandings and disappointments; that’s just part of the journey. The important thing is to keep coming back—to the table, to the conversation, to each other.
He reminds Su Yen that family isn’t just about shared blood. It’s about the stories you tell, the values you hold, and the dreams you share. It’s about showing up for each other, even when it’s tough or inconvenient. In a world that often celebrates going it alone, he hopes she’ll remember the quiet strength that comes from knowing she belongs to something bigger than herself.
